source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Unit 7 (PDF 220-233, printed 218-231); not printed in the book. Based on the unit's text, theorems, formulas and worked examples (changed values); none repeats the unit's exercises. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Unit 7 (Kinematics of Motion in a Straight Line (TOC: 'Kinematics')), arranged by the unit's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation that shows the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the motion of objects:

options.text: only by the forces acting on them
only when they are at rest
without considering the causes of motion

blocks.explanation: Kinematics describes position, velocity and acceleration; it does not ask what causes the motion.

book_ref.quote: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the motion of objects without considering the causes of motion.

blocks.prompt: 2 The motion of a particle along a straight line is called:
blocks.explanation: By definition, motion along a straight line is rectilinear motion.

book_ref.quote: The motion of a particle along a straight line is called rectilinear motion.

blocks.prompt: 3 Which one of the following is an example of rectilinear motion?

options.text: A lift going up and down its shaft
The blade of a turning ceiling fan
A satellite going round the Earth
A child on a moving merry-go-round

blocks.explanation: In rectilinear motion the particle moves only forwards or backwards along one fixed line. A lift moves along one vertical line; the others move along curves.

book_ref.quote: the particle moves only forwards or backwards along one fixed line

blocks.prompt: 4 Which one of the following is a scalar quantity?
blocks.explanation: A scalar is completely described by magnitude only. Speed has no direction; velocity, displacement and acceleration are vectors.

book_ref.quote: Scalar quantities are those that are completely described by magnitude only

blocks.prompt: 5 A speed of \(72\) km/h is equal to:
blocks.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{5}{18}\): \(72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 20\) m/s.

book_ref.quote: Its common units are m/s and km/h.

blocks.prompt: 6 A speed of \(15\) m/s is equal to:
blocks.explanation: Multiply by \(\frac{18}{5}\): \(15 \times \frac{18}{5} = 54\) km/h. (Multiplying by \(\frac{5}{18}\) instead gives the wrong \(\frac{25}{6}\).)

book_ref.quote: Speed: Rate at which distance is covered per unit time, irrespective of direction.

blocks.prompt: 7 The distance travelled by a moving particle:

options.text: can be negative when it moves backwards
is always zero for a return trip
depends only on the initial and final positions

blocks.explanation: Distance is the total length of the path travelled, regardless of direction, so it is never negative and it never decreases.

book_ref.quote: Distance: Total length of the path travelled, regardless of direction.

blocks.prompt: 8 Which one of the following sets contains only vector quantities?
blocks.explanation: Displacement, velocity and acceleration have both magnitude and direction. Distance, speed and time are scalars.

book_ref.quote: Vector quantities are described by both magnitude and direction.

blocks.prompt: 9 A girl walks \(5\) m east and then \(12\) m west along a straight road. Her displacement is:
blocks.explanation: Taking east as positive: \(5 + (-12) = -7\) m, i.e. \(7\) m west. (\(17\) m is the distance, not the displacement.)

book_ref.quote: Displacement is change in position of a particle represented by a vector from initial to final position.

blocks.prompt: 10 A swimmer swims from one end of a \(50\) m straight pool to the other end and back, two times. His distance and displacement are:
blocks.explanation: Each length is \(50\) m and he swims \(4\) lengths: distance \(= 4 \times 50 = 200\) m. He ends where he started, so displacement \(= 0\).

book_ref.quote: Depends on the path taken

blocks.prompt: 11 Speed is:

options.text: the rate of change of velocity

blocks.explanation: Velocity is a vector and its magnitude gives speed.

book_ref.quote: It is vector quantity and its magnitude gives speed.

blocks.prompt: 12 The rate of change of velocity with respect to time, including direction, is called:
blocks.explanation: By definition acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time; it is a vector.

book_ref.quote: Acceleration: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, including direction.

blocks.prompt: 13 The average velocity of an object is defined as:
blocks.explanation: Average velocity uses displacement; total distance over total time is the average speed.

book_ref.quote: defined as the total displacement divided by the total time taken

blocks.prompt: 14 A cyclist rides \(150\) m north in \(30\) s and then \(50\) m south in \(20\) s along a straight road. His average speed is:
blocks.explanation: Total distance \(= 150 + 50 = 200\) m, total time \(= 50\) s, average speed \(= \frac{200}{50} = 4\) m/s. (The average of the two speeds, \(\frac{5 + 2.5}{2} = 3.75\), is wrong.)

book_ref.quote: The average speed of an object is defined as the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken:

blocks.prompt: 15 For the same cyclist (\(150\) m north in \(30\) s, then \(50\) m south in \(20\) s), the average velocity is:
blocks.explanation: With north positive, displacement \(= 150 - 50 = 100\) m; average velocity \(= \frac{100}{50} = 2\) m/s, positive, so towards the north.

book_ref.quote: Taking east as positive and west as negative:

blocks.prompt: 16 The position of a particle is \(x(t) = 2t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 12t\) (\(x\) in m, \(t\) in s). Its velocity at \(t = 3\) s is:

book_ref.quote: is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time at a given instant

blocks.prompt: 17 For \(x(t) = 2t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 12t\), the particle is momentarily at rest at:

book_ref.quote: momentarily at rest (this is where a particle can turn back)

blocks.prompt: 18 A particle moves so that \(x(t) = t^{2} - 8t\) (m, s). Its speed at \(t = 2\) s is:
blocks.explanation: \(v = 2t - 8\), \(v(2) = -4\) m/s; speed \(= |v| = 4\) m/s. Speed is never negative.

book_ref.quote: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity

blocks.prompt: 19 If \(x(t) = t^{3} - 4t^{2} + 5\) (m, s), the acceleration at \(t = 2\) s is:

book_ref.quote: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time is called acceleration.

blocks.prompt: 20 The velocity of a particle in terms of its displacement is \(v = 2x + 3\). Its acceleration when \(x = 1\) is:
blocks.explanation: Here \(v\) is a function of \(x\), so \(a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = (2x + 3)(2)\); at \(x = 1\): \(a = 5 \times 2 = 10\). (\(2\) is only \(\frac{dv}{dx}\).)

book_ref.quote: of the particle is given as a function of displacement

blocks.prompt: 21 If displacement is measured in metres and time in seconds, the unit of acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: Acceleration is change of velocity (m/s) per second: \(\frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}} = \text{m/s}^{2}\).

book_ref.quote: then unit of acceleration is meters per second square

blocks.prompt: 22 At some instant a particle has \(v = 5\) m/s and \(a = -3\) m/s\(^{2}\). At that instant the particle is:

options.text: moving in the positive direction and speeding up
moving in the negative direction and slowing down
moving in the positive direction and slowing down

blocks.explanation: \(v > 0\): moving in the positive direction. \(v\) and \(a\) have opposite signs, so the particle is slowing down.

book_ref.quote: so the particle is speeding up in the negative direction

blocks.prompt: 23 For any journey along a straight line, which statement is always true?
blocks.explanation: Since \(|\text{displacement}| \le \text{distance}\), dividing by the same total time gives \(|\text{average velocity}| \le \text{average speed}\); equality holds only if the particle never turns back.

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of the average velocity can never be more than the average speed

blocks.prompt: 24 The slope of a displacement-time graph represents the:
blocks.explanation: Slope \(= \frac{dx}{dt}\), which is the velocity.

book_ref.quote: represents velocity of the particle.

blocks.prompt: 25 A horizontal straight segment on a displacement-time graph shows that the particle is:
blocks.explanation: Horizontal means \(x\) does not change, so \(v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0\): the particle is at rest.

book_ref.quote: the particle is at rest and the displacement-time graph is a horizontal line

blocks.prompt: 26 A displacement-time graph is a straight line from \((0, 0)\) to \((4, 20)\) (\(t\) in s, \(x\) in m). The velocity is:
blocks.explanation: Velocity \(=\) slope \(= \frac{20 - 0}{4 - 0} = 5\) m/s. (\(0.2\) is the slope taken upside down.)

book_ref.quote: the displacement-time graph is a straight line.

blocks.prompt: 27 On a displacement-time graph a straight segment falls from \((2, 30)\) to \((5, 0)\) (\(t\) in h, \(x\) in km). The velocity on this segment is:
blocks.explanation: Slope \(= \frac{0 - 30}{5 - 2} = -10\) km/h. The minus sign means motion in the negative direction.

book_ref.quote: the particle moves in the opposite direction, and the displacement time graph is a falling straight line

blocks.prompt: 28 A displacement-time graph joins \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(10, 3)\), \(B(25, 3)\), \(C(35, 0)\) with straight lines (\(t\) in minutes, \(x\) in km). The average speed for the whole journey is:
blocks.explanation: Distance \(= 3 + 3 = 6\) km in \(35\) min (the stop counts): \(\frac{6}{35} \times 60 = \frac{72}{7} \approx 10.29\) km/h. (\(0\) is the average velocity.)

book_ref.quote: Waiting time counts in the total time of a journey.

blocks.prompt: 29 For the same graph \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(10, 3)\), \(B(25, 3)\), \(C(35, 0)\) (minutes, km), the velocity from \(B\) to \(C\) is:
blocks.explanation: Slope \(= \frac{0 - 3}{35 - 25} = -0.3\) km/min \(= -0.3 \times 60 = -18\) km/h (negative slope: moving back).

book_ref.quote: Positive slope: forward motion. Negative slope: backward motion.

blocks.prompt: 30 If a displacement-time graph is a curve, the velocity at an instant is:

options.text: the slope of the tangent at that point
the height of the graph at that point
the area under the graph up to that point

blocks.explanation: For a curve the velocity keeps changing; at an instant it is \(\frac{dx}{dt}\), the slope of the tangent.

book_ref.quote: the velocity at an instant is the slope of the tangent at that point

blocks.prompt: 31 The slope of a velocity-time graph represents the:
blocks.explanation: Slope \(= \frac{dv}{dt}\), which is the acceleration.

book_ref.quote: represents acceleration of the particle.

blocks.prompt: 32 The area under a velocity-time graph (above the time axis) between two instants gives the:
blocks.explanation: Area \(= \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} v\,dt = x(t_{2}) - x(t_{1})\), the displacement.

book_ref.quote: Displacement = Area under velocity-time graph

blocks.prompt: 33 A horizontal straight segment on a velocity-time graph shows that the particle is moving with:
blocks.explanation: Horizontal means \(v\) is constant, so \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 0\): uniform velocity, not rest.

book_ref.quote: the velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line

blocks.prompt: 34 A velocity-time graph is a straight line from \((0, 4)\) to \((6, 16)\) (\(t\) in s, \(v\) in m/s). The acceleration is:
blocks.explanation: \(a = \) slope \(= \frac{16 - 4}{6 - 0} = 2\) m/s\(^{2}\). (\(\frac{8}{3} = \frac{16}{6}\) forgets the starting velocity.)

book_ref.quote: is moving with constant acceleration, its velocity-time graph is a straight line

blocks.prompt: 35 For the same graph (straight line from \((0, 4)\) to \((6, 16)\), m/s and s), the displacement in the \(6\) s is:
blocks.explanation: Area of the trapezium \(= \frac{1}{2}(4 + 16) \times 6 = 60\) m.

book_ref.quote: displacement of the particle during the time interval from

blocks.prompt: 36 A velocity-time graph encloses an area \(A_{1} = 30\) m above the time axis and \(A_{2} = 12\) m below it. The distance travelled is:
blocks.explanation: Distance \(= A_{1} + A_{2} = 30 + 12 = 42\) m (displacement would be \(A_{1} - A_{2} = 18\) m).

book_ref.quote: is the area below time axis and graph

blocks.prompt: 37 A particle's velocity falls uniformly from \(20\) m/s at \(t = 0\) to \(-8\) m/s at \(t = 7\) s. Its displacement in these \(7\) s is:

book_ref.quote: If velocity-time graph lies both above and below the time axis

blocks.prompt: 38 A particle starts from rest, reaches \(10\) m/s uniformly at \(t = 4\) s, keeps this velocity until \(t = 14\) s and then comes to rest uniformly at \(t = 18\) s. Its displacement is:
blocks.explanation: Trapezium with parallel sides \(18\) and \(10\), height \(10\): \(\frac{1}{2}(18 + 10) \times 10 = 140\) m.

book_ref.quote: A trapezium (trapezoid) is a four-sided plane figure that has exactly one pair of parallel sides.

blocks.prompt: 39 For the same particle (\(10\) m/s from \(t = 4\) s to \(t = 14\) s, rest at \(t = 18\) s), the acceleration in the last \(4\) s is:

book_ref.quote: the particle is moving with uniform negative acceleration (retardation)

blocks.prompt: 40 A velocity-time graph which is a curve (not a straight line) shows that the particle is moving with:
blocks.explanation: A straight line has the same slope everywhere; a curve has a changing slope, i.e. a variable acceleration.

book_ref.quote: then its velocity-time graph is not a straight line

blocks.prompt: 41 The velocity of a particle is \(v(t) = 3t^{2}\) m/s. Its displacement from \(t = 1\) s to \(t = 3\) s is:

book_ref.quote: Adding all strips is exactly what the integral

blocks.prompt: 42 The equations \(v = u + at\), \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) and \(2ax = v^{2} - u^{2}\) can be used only when:
blocks.explanation: They were derived by integrating \(\frac{dv}{dt} = a\) with \(a\) constant; for variable acceleration we integrate directly.

book_ref.quote: These three equations are valid only when the acceleration is constant.

blocks.prompt: 43 Integrating \(\frac{dv}{dt} = a\) (constant) gives \(v = at + c\). With \(v = u\) at \(t = 0\), the constant \(c\) equals:

book_ref.quote: So the constant is just the starting velocity

blocks.prompt: 44 The equation of motion that does not contain the time \(t\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(2ax = v^{2} - u^{2}\) comes from eliminating \(t\) between \(v = u + at\) and \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\).

book_ref.quote: Substitute this into equation (4) to eliminate

blocks.prompt: 45 A car moving at \(4\) m/s accelerates uniformly at \(2.5\) m/s\(^{2}\) for \(6\) s. Its velocity at the end is:
blocks.explanation: \(v = u + at = 4 + 2.5 \times 6 = 19\) m/s. (\(15\) forgets \(u\); \(69\) m is the distance.)

book_ref.quote: These equations are frequently used to describe and analyze the motion of a particle under constant acceleration.

blocks.prompt: 46 A train starts from rest with a uniform acceleration of \(0.5\) m/s\(^{2}\). The distance covered in \(40\) s is:
blocks.explanation: \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2} = 0 + \frac{1}{2}(0.5)(1600) = 400\) m. (\(800\) forgets the \(\frac{1}{2}\); \(20\) m/s is the final velocity.)

book_ref.quote: Each equation links four of the five quantities

blocks.prompt: 47 A car moving at \(25\) m/s is brought to rest with uniform retardation in a distance of \(50\) m. Its acceleration is:

book_ref.quote: Find the quantity that is neither given nor asked, and pick the equation that does not contain it

blocks.prompt: 48 A motorbike speeds up uniformly from \(6\) m/s to \(14\) m/s while covering \(40\) m. Its acceleration is:

book_ref.quote: By simplification, we get:

blocks.prompt: 49 In deriving \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\), the constant of integration \(c_{1}\) comes out zero because:

options.text: every constant of integration is zero
the starting point is taken as \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\)

blocks.explanation: Putting \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\) in \(x = ut + \frac{a t^{2}}{2} + c_{1}\) gives \(c_{1} = 0\). If the particle started at \(x_{0}\), we would get \(c_{1} = x_{0}\).

book_ref.quote: because we chose the starting point

blocks.prompt: 50 A particle has acceleration \(a(t) = 6t\) m/s\(^{2}\) and velocity \(2\) m/s at \(t = 0\). Its velocity at \(t = 2\) s is:

book_ref.quote: For variable acceleration integrate:

blocks.prompt: 51 A particle starts from rest at \(t = 0\) with acceleration \(a(t) = \sin t\). Its velocity is:

book_ref.quote: In Examples 9 and 10 the acceleration changes with time

blocks.prompt: 52 The velocity of a particle is \(v(t) = 4 - 2t\) m/s and \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\). Its position at \(t = 3\) s is:

book_ref.quote: integration recovers a quantity from its rate

blocks.text: 7.1.7 Motion of a Free Particle Moving Along a Vertical Line

blocks.prompt: 53 In free vertical motion the acceleration due to gravity is taken as:
blocks.explanation: The book takes \(g \approx 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\) (air resistance neglected).

book_ref.quote: The acceleration due to gravity is denoted by

blocks.prompt: 54 At the highest point of a ball thrown vertically upward:

options.text: \(v\) is maximum and the acceleration is \(0\)

blocks.explanation: The velocity becomes zero at the highest point, but gravity still acts: the acceleration is \(g\) downwards.

book_ref.quote: becomes zero at the highest point

blocks.prompt: 55 A stone is dropped from a high bridge. Its speed after \(2.5\) s is:
blocks.explanation: \(v = u + gt = 0 + 9.8 \times 2.5 = 24.5\) m/s. (\(30.625\) m is the distance fallen.)

book_ref.quote: If the particle moves downward, it accelerates toward the ground at the rate

blocks.prompt: 56 A ball is thrown vertically upward with \(14.7\) m/s. The time to reach the highest point is:

book_ref.quote: If a particle is projected upward, its velocity decreases uniformly due to gravity

blocks.prompt: 57 The maximum height reached by a ball thrown vertically upward with \(19.6\) m/s is:

book_ref.quote: When a particle moves under the influence of gravity alone and air resistance is neglected

blocks.prompt: 58 For a particle moving vertically upward (upward taken as positive), the velocity after time \(t\) is:
blocks.explanation: For upward motion \(a = -g\), so \(v = u + (-g)t = u - gt\).

book_ref.quote: Rising: gravity acts against the motion

blocks.prompt: 59 A stone is dropped from the top of a tower \(78.4\) m high. The time it takes to reach the ground is:

book_ref.quote: means released without a push
